adversarial_critique: Claude's core numerical extraction and Unfavourable direction for Private sector ownership (1 = investor-owned [n = 58] vs. 0 = government-owned [n = 321] or cooperative [n = 121], total N = 500; PDF p. 6) accurately reflect Table 2 (PDF p. 9), where private ownership is associated with a +$144.04 higher annual water bill (std. coeff. 0.35, p < 0.01) and a +1.55 percentage-point higher water bill share for lowest-quintile households (std. coeff. 0.26, p < 0.01). Outcome polarity is unambiguous (higher = worse affordability for both outcomes), and the PDF font-encoding defect that drops minus signs on negative covariates in Table 2 (e.g., Groundwater printed as 46.97** and Service population (ln) as 10.96, alongside the footnote typo '**p , 0.0' for p < 0.01) does not affect Private sector, whose positive signs are verified by prose on PDF p. 8 ('$144 higher', '1.55% more') and unadjusted group means on PDF p. 6 ($501 vs. $315; 4.39% vs. 2.84%). However, Claude's exposure_full and raw_direction_text overreach by bundling investor ownership with state PUC cost-of-service regulation and NJ/PA fair-value and DSIC statutes and asserting that pro-private regulation is associated with 'lower affordability'. In Table 2 (PDF p. 9), Favorable private regulation (1 = NJ, PA)—a two-state dummy spanning 17 private and 18 public systems (Table 3, PDF p. 10)—raises annual bills (+$88.64**, p < 0.01) but is statistically null on lowest-quintile income share (+0.46, p >= 0.05), while PUC regulates public utilities is null on both price (36.43) and affordability (0.29; PDF p. 8) and private PUC regulation is unestimated because all 58 private utilities are PUC-regulated (PDF p. 7). Finally, Unfavourable holds cleanly when Family C fixes the exposure pole to private ownership, whereas flipping the cross-sectional contrast to public/cooperative ownership flips the valence to Favourable (PDF p. 9; alternative_substantive_direction was left blank), and outcomes reflect standardized 60,000 gal/year tariff schedules excluding low-income assistance discounts and wastewater fees (PDF pp. 5-6).

evidence_quotes.quote: Privately owned water systems have higher water prices and are less affordable.
Among the 500 water systems in our study, 321 are government-owned, 121 are cooperative
privately owned water systems, low-income households spend 1.55% more of their income on their water bills.
Only six states regulate public systems, but this has no effect on price or affordability.

numerical_check_note: All stored point estimates, standardized coefficients, significance levels, and sample counts match the paper exactly: N = 500 systems (58 investor-owned vs. 442 public [321 government-owned + 121 cooperative], PDF p. 6); Private sector OLS Coeff. = 144.04** (std. coeff. 0.35**) for annual water bill and 1.55** (std. coeff. 0.26**) for lowest-quintile income share spent on water (Table 2, PDF p. 9; prose rounds to $144 on PDF p. 8); Favorable private regulation (1 = NJ, PA) Coeff. = 88.64** (std. coeff. 0.17**) for annual bill and non-significant 0.46 (std. coeff. 0.06) for income share. Standard errors and CIs are genuinely omitted in Table 2 (which also has a journal footnote typo '**p , 0.0' for p < 0.01 and dropped minus signs on negative covariates in the PDF text layer).
polarity_or_orientation_issue: Outcome polarity is straightforward ('higher = worse' for both annual water bill in USD and lowest-quintile household income share spent on water), so positive coefficients (+144.04**, +1.55**) validly map to Unfavourable for investor-owned utilities. Two orientation/bundling nuances warrant attention: (1) symmetric public-vs-private cross-sectional pole orientation—Table 2 codes Private sector = 1 vs. Public = 0 (Unfavourable), whereas framing public/cooperative ownership as the exposure flips the direction to Favourable (PDF p. 9: 'public ownership is related to lower prices'), and Claude left alternative_substantive_direction blank under 'as reported'; (2) exposure_full and raw_direction_text conflate private ownership with PUC regulation and NJ/PA fair-value/DSIC laws, even though Favorable private regulation (NJ, PA) is null on lowest-quintile affordability (+0.46, ns) and PUC regulation of public utilities is null on both outcomes (+36.43, +0.29, ns).
